planting.note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation.

directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2007 and quickly becoming one of the most sought-after and widely used hop varieties in modern craft brewing, this vigorous climbing bine produces resinous, aromatic cones with a distinctive tropical fruit, citrus, and gooseberry character that helped define the juicy, hazy IPA styles that have dominated craft beer for over a decade. Like other hops it is a perennial vine that dies back to the ground each winter and regrows vigorously each spring, needing a sturdy tall support and full sun to reach its full trellis height and cone production. Train young bines up the support as they grow, harvest cones in late summer when they feel dry and papery and spring back after being squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for the best cone development.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost. Native to and named for the region around Kalamata, Greece, this classic dual-purpose olive cultivar produces large, almond-shaped, deep purple-black fruit famous worldwide when brine-cured for eating, along with good-quality oil, making it one of the most recognizable named table olive varieties globally. Like other olives it thrives on neglect once established, tolerating poor, rocky, alkaline soil and long dry summers far better than regular watering and rich soil, and needs a genuinely Mediterranean-type climate with wet winters and hot, dry summers to fruit and ripen well. Raw olives straight from the tree are intensely bitter and inedible; fruit must be cured through brining, salt-curing, or lye processing before eating, a process requiring several weeks depending on the method used.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Considered the finest-flavored and rarest of the three main cacao varieties, Criollo (Spanish for 'native' or 'creole') produces pale, thin-shelled pods with mild, complex, low-bitterness flavor prized by fine chocolate makers, but the tree is notably more susceptible to disease and lower-yielding than the hardier Forastero variety that dominates most commercial cacao production worldwide. It requires the warm, humid, sheltered understory conditions of a tropical rainforest, ideally grown beneath taller shade trees, and demands more careful disease management than more robust cacao types, making it a specialty planting for dedicated chocolate enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors rather than an easy home crop. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Forastero cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Forastero cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. The hardiest, highest-yielding, and by far the most widely grown of the main cacao varieties, accounting for the large majority of the world's chocolate supply, it produces thick-shelled pods with a stronger, more straightforwardly bitter and less nuanced flavor than the rarer Criollo type, but far better disease resistance and productivity that make it the backbone of commercial cacao farming across West Africa and Brazil. Easier to grow than Criollo, it still requires the same warm, humid, shaded rainforest understory conditions typical of all cacao, ideally interplanted beneath taller banana or other shade trees as is traditional in cacao agroforestry systems. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity and its first pod harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Named for the former French colonial name of Réunion Island, where it was first cultivated after being introduced from Yemen, this historic Arabica coffee variety is one of the parent lines behind many modern specialty coffee cultivars and is still prized by growers and roasters for producing sweet, well-balanced, complex cups, though its lower yield compared to newer hybrid varieties has made it less common in large-scale commercial production. Like other Arabica coffees it grows best in the dappled shade of taller companion trees, mimicking its native highland forest understory habitat, and needs consistent warmth and moisture without ever standing in wet, waterlogged soil. Water regularly but ensure good drainage, provide filtered shade, and expect the first coffee cherry harvest after three to four years of growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Considered the original Arabica coffee variety from which nearly all other Arabica cultivars ultimately descend, having spread from Yemen through European colonial cultivation to become the ancestral genetic base of the world's coffee industry, it is still valued today for its classically sweet, clean, well-balanced cup quality despite its taller, more open growth habit and lower yield and disease resistance compared to modern hybrids. Its lanky, open branching habit and susceptibility to coffee leaf rust and other diseases have led most commercial growers to switch to higher-yielding, more disease-resistant hybrid varieties, but heirloom Typica plantings remain prized by specialty coffee producers for their traditional flavor profile. Provide the same dappled shade, consistent moisture, and good drainage other Arabica coffees need, and expect the first harvest after three to four years of growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
